title: MTRX™ Field Series No. 06 · Read the room · Kevin Cecil

cards.name: Why this guide exists
cards.q: What does this guide treat every read of a person as?
options: A verdict you can act on
A hypothesis you test by asking
cards.why: Notice, guess, ask, update. A read you never check is just a story you like.

cards.name: Why this guide exists
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Why this guide exists" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I don't read minds. I read changes, then I ask."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: In real time, how often do people correctly judge whether someone is lying or telling the truth?
cards.why: Bond and DePaulo 2006, 24,483 judges: 54%. Stop 1.1.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: Compared with students, how good are police and other professionals at spotting lies?
cards.why: About 54.5% vs 54.1% (Aamodt and Custer 2006). Stop 1.1.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: "Communication is 7% words, 38% tone and 55% body language." That rule is...
options: A narrow 1967 result about feelings when words and tone clash
cards.why: Mehrabian rejects the general use. Stop 1.4.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: Someone looks up and to the right while answering. That tells you...
cards.why: The NLP eye claim failed in three studies (Wiseman et al. 2012). Stop 1.3.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: A clinic owner sounds nervous on your call. Most likely meaning?
options: Nothing specific: stress has many causes
cards.why: Reading stress as lying is the Othello error. Stop 1.3.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: Best way to understand what a client wants?
options: Imagine yourself in their shoes, carefully
cards.why: Across 25 experiments, asking beat imagining (Eyal, Steffel and Epley 2018). Stop 1.8.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: After a first conversation, people usually like you...
options: About as much as you think
cards.why: The liking gap (Boothby et al. 2018). Stop 1.11.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: When you're nervous presenting, how visible is it?
options: Exactly as visible as it feels
cards.why: The illusion of transparency (Gilovich et al. 1998). Stop 1.11.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: A psychic says "you're independent, but sometimes you doubt yourself" and it feels spot on. Why?
cards.why: A Barnum statement. Stop 1.9.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: Which trait do strangers judge most accurately from a first impression?
cards.why: Visible traits read best (Borkenau and Liebler 1992). Stop 1.2.

cards.name: Your baseline: ten questions first
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Your baseline: ten questions first" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I tested my instincts before I trusted them."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The 54% problem
cards.q: Across 24,483 judges, what was the average accuracy at telling lies from truths in real time?
cards.why: Bond and DePaulo 2006. Lies were caught 47% of the time, truths 61%: we lean toward believing.

cards.name: The 54% problem
cards.q: Your caller is 'sure' a clinic owner lied about having no budget. What does research say about that sureness?
cards.why: DePaulo et al. 1997. Check the budget with a question, not a gut call.

cards.name: The 54% problem
cards.q: Why did Bond's read of Le Chiffre's tell cost him?
options: A visible tell can be faked by someone who knows you're watching
cards.why: A cue you can see, the other side can plant. Treat it as a hypothesis to test.

cards.name: The 54% problem
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The 54% problem" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Most people can't spot a lie much better than a coin flip, so I don't guess. I ask and I check."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: First impressions: fast, sticky, half right
cards.q: People shown a face for 100 milliseconds...
options: Form impressions that match their unlimited-time judgments
Are more accurate than with longer looks
cards.why: Willis and Todorov 2006. Longer looks mostly raise confidence, not accuracy.

cards.name: First impressions: fast, sticky, half right
cards.q: Which trait do strangers judge most accurately at first sight?
cards.why: Visible traits leak into behaviour; honesty and intelligence mostly don't (Borkenau and Liebler 1992).

cards.name: First impressions: fast, sticky, half right
cards.q: A safari operator sounds cold for the first 30 seconds of a call. Best move?
options: Note it as a guess and keep gathering
cards.why: Thin slices carry some signal and a lot of noise. Let later behaviour update the read.

cards.name: First impressions: fast, sticky, half right
cards.q: Page closed: explain "First impressions: fast, sticky, half right" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "First impressions are fast and they agree with each other. That doesn't make them right, so I hold mine loosely."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Baselines: read the change, not the tell
cards.q: In DePaulo's meta-analysis of 158 possible lie cues, what did they find?
options: A few cues reliably reveal lies
Most cues are weak or unrelated to lying
Eye contact is the best cue
cards.why: 1,338 estimates, 120 samples. There is no single tell.

cards.name: Baselines: read the change, not the tell
cards.q: A clinic owner tenses up when you ask about his current website. Most defensible read?
options: The topic matters to him somehow: ask
He wants to end the call
cards.why: Stress has many causes. Reading it as lying is the Othello error. Name it and ask.

cards.name: Baselines: read the change, not the tell
cards.q: Why did the three fingers give Hicox away?
options: It broke the German way of counting from the thumb
He held eye contact too long
cards.why: A culture mismatch, not a lie cue. Context is part of every baseline.

cards.name: Baselines: read the change, not the tell
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Baselines: read the change, not the tell" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I don't trust tells. I watch for change from someone's normal, and then I ask about it."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The five channels
cards.q: The '7% words, 38% tone, 55% body' rule is...
options: A narrow 1967 finding about feelings when words and tone conflict
cards.why: Mehrabian's studies used single words about liking. He rejects the general use.

cards.name: The five channels
cards.q: For catching deception, training on which channel works better?
cards.why: Hauch et al. 2014: verbal content training had the larger effects.

cards.name: The five channels
cards.q: A prospect says 'sounds good' after a long pause, in a flat voice, then changes topic. Best move?
options: Ask about the gap between words and tone
Trust the words, ignore the rest
cards.why: When channels disagree, ask. 'Sounds good, or sounds like a lot?'

cards.name: The five channels
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The five channels" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Words carry more than people think. I listen to what someone chooses to say, then check it against how they say it."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Warmth first, then competence
cards.q: In the warmth and competence research, which tends to weigh more in overall impressions?
cards.why: Warmth (intent) comes first and weighs more (Wojciszke 1998; Fiske et al. 2007).

cards.name: Warmth first, then competence
cards.q: Babyfaced adults tend to be seen as...
options: Warmer but less powerful and competent
cards.why: Zebrowitz 2017. The job is showing competence: proof, pace, preparation.

cards.name: Warmth first, then competence
cards.q: Which competence signal has evidence behind it but does NOT prove real ability?
cards.why: Speaking time predicts who emerges as leader, not who leads well. Use real proof too.

cards.name: Warmth first, then competence
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Warmth first, then competence" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "People decide if you're on their side before they decide if you're good. So I show I care first, then I show proof."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: What people want
cards.q: Asking a prospect for advice tends to make you look...
options: More competent, especially on hard questions
cards.why: Brooks, Gino and Schweitzer 2015.

cards.name: What people want
cards.q: In ultimatum games, why do people turn down free money?
options: They reject unfair offers even at a cost
cards.why: Fairness is a want you can't ignore, especially in pricing.

cards.name: What people want
cards.q: A clinic owner says 'my last agency took my money and vanished'. Which want is loudest?
cards.why: Fairness. Answer it head on: milestones, what he owns, how he can leave.

cards.name: What people want
cards.q: Page closed: explain "What people want" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Most people aren't buying the website. They're buying respect, control or a fair deal, so I listen for which one."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Reading power in a room
cards.q: Cheng et al. 2013 found two routes to status. Which pair?
cards.why: Dominance works through fear, prestige through respected expertise. Both raise influence.

cards.name: Reading power in a room
cards.q: Per eye-tracking research, the best clue to who holds status in a meeting is...
options: Who others look at, beyond who's speaking
cards.why: Foulsham et al. 2010: high-status people get looked at more often and for longer.

cards.name: Reading power in a room
cards.q: The famous claim that power makes people worse at perspective taking...
options: Failed a large replication for the sarcasm task
cards.why: Many Labs 3: 2,969 people, d = .03 vs the original .77.

cards.name: Reading power in a room
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Reading power in a room" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I don't look for the loudest person. I watch where the eyes go when something important is said."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Ask, don't guess
cards.q: Across 25 experiments, what improved accuracy about another person's mind?
cards.why: Eyal, Steffel and Epley 2018: perspective getting, not taking.

cards.name: Ask, don't guess
cards.q: Which questions most increased liking in Huang et al. 2017?
cards.why: Follow-ups show you listened (d = .35).

cards.name: Ask, don't guess
cards.q: You know websites; a dentist doesn't. Which bias makes you overestimate what he understands?
cards.why: Once you know something, it's hard to imagine not knowing it. Check with a question.

cards.name: Ask, don't guess
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Ask, don't guess" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I'd rather ask one good question than guess right. Guessing feels smart; asking actually is."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Cold reading, decoded
cards.q: In Forer's demonstration, 39 students got the same sketch. How accurate did they rate it?
cards.why: About 4.26 of 5. Vague, flattering statements fit nearly everyone.

cards.name: Cold reading, decoded
cards.q: 'You can be outgoing, but you also need time alone.' Which technique?
cards.why: A trait and its opposite can't miss.

cards.name: Cold reading, decoded
cards.q: What's the honest twin of a cold read?
options: An observation turned into a question you verify
cards.why: Same observation, checked instead of faked.

cards.name: Cold reading, decoded
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Cold reading, decoded" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "If a read would fit almost anyone, it isn't a read. I turn my guesses into questions."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Reading the phone and the DM
cards.q: Recruiters heard or read the same pitches. Hearing them led to...
options: Higher ratings of intellect and hireability
cards.why: Schroeder and Epley 2015: intellect effect d = 1.16 for recruiters.

cards.name: Reading the phone and the DM
cards.q: Why do sarcastic emails misfire more than senders expect?
options: Senders hear their own tone; readers don't
cards.why: Kruger et al. 2005: egocentrism over email.

cards.name: Reading the phone and the DM
cards.q: A safari operator takes six hours to reply. What does the evidence say this means?
cards.why: Reply time isn't a validated signal. Follow up on substance.

cards.name: Reading the phone and the DM
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Reading the phone and the DM" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Text loses tone, so anything warm goes in a voice note and anything important gets a direct question."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: How you read to others
cards.q: Speakers told about the illusion of transparency before a speech...
options: Were more composed and gave better speeches
cards.why: Savitsky and Gilovich 2003.

cards.name: How you read to others
cards.q: After a first conversation, people usually...
options: Overestimate how much they were liked
Underestimate how much they were liked
cards.why: The liking gap (Boothby et al. 2018).

cards.name: How you read to others
cards.q: Saying 'I'm not sure, let me check' to a client is judged...
options: More harshly by you than by them
cards.why: The beautiful mess effect (Bruk et al. 2018).

cards.name: How you read to others
cards.q: Page closed: explain "How you read to others" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "My nerves are louder inside my head than on my face. People notice far less than I fear."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The calibration log
cards.q: When can you trust a gut call, per Kahneman and Klein 2009?
options: In regular settings with lots of practice and fast, clear feedback
cards.why: Confidence isn't the test. Regularity plus feedback is.

cards.name: The calibration log
cards.q: You said 90% a prospect would book; they didn't. Your Brier score for it?
cards.why: (0.9 minus 0) squared = 0.81. Overconfidence gets punished, which is the point.

cards.name: The calibration log
cards.q: Which feedback improved forecasters most (Lichtenstein and Fischhoff 1980)?
options: How often their 70% calls came true
cards.why: Calibration feedback works; outcome-only feedback barely does.

cards.name: The calibration log
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The calibration log" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I write down my read before the meeting and score it after. That's the only way a gut gets better."
cards.label: Say it in the room
